documents.title: Health at a Glance Indicators Report

chunks.content: KEY POINTS Early childhood screening for type 1 diabetes provides an opportunity to identify individuals with presymptomatic, early-stage disease and intervene to prevent diabetic ketoacidosis. Mixed methods were used to explore multilevel barriers and facilitators to type 1 diabetes autoantibody screening in pediatric well-child visits, and, more broadly, the implementation outcomes of acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility. Most parents and clinicians who participated in this study found type 1 diabetes screening during pediatric well-child visits to be acceptable and appropriate. Implementation barriers (e.g., costs) and facilitators (e.g., education) were identified. Screening for type 1 diabetes within pediatric well-child visits could be a viable strategy if implementation strategies address identified barriers and promote facilitators. Type 1 diabetes is a chronic disease with potential for life-threatening outcomes if not diagnosed promptly and managed properly. In individuals with type 1 diabetes, the immune system attacks the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, eventually leading to a depletion of insulin and abnormally elevated levels of blood glucose. Patients with type 1 diabetes typically present in the symptomatic stage (stage 3) of the disease, and up to 58% of patients present with potentially life-threatening diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) ( ). DKA often requires hospitalization, has a mortality rate of 0.15–0.31% in children ( ), and, at the time of type 1 diabetes diagnosis, is associated with significant health care costs ( ) and poorer long-term glycemic control ( ). A single episode of moderate to severe DKA in a young child has also been associated with lower cognitive scores and altered brain growth ( ). Pancreatic autoantibodies (insulin autoantibodies, glutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibodies, insulinoma antigen-2 autoantibodies, and zinc transporter 8 autoantibodies) are markers for disease and offer a potential avenue for early identification and monitoring of at-risk individuals and those with presymptomatic, early-stage (stage 1 and 2) type 1 diabetes ( , ). Implementation of disease screenings can enable preventive strategies or earlier diagnoses, leading to increased quality of life, fewer severe outcomes, and reduced medical costs. These benefits are reflected by the increase in population screening efforts in health care settings in the United States ( ) and have been demonstrated in some existing type 1 diabetes screening efforts. For example, autoantibody screening has been shown to significantly reduce the rate of DKA at diagnosis ( , ), thus avoiding the risk for serious complications and mortality associated with DKA and reducing the burden on the health care system ( ). Screening for type 1 diabetes also permits the provision of early education and psychosocial support ( ); enables access to emerging therapies to modulate the immune response, potentially delaying the onset of clinical (stage 3) disease ( , ); and, after clinical type 1 diabetes diagnosis, can result in improved glycemic control ( ) and psychosocial outcomes, including diabetes quality of life and lower parental stress ( ). A recent study estimated that population screening via autoantibody testing would cost ∼$141 per patient based on Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services laboratory fees and required clinician time discussing testing, collecting samples, and communicating results ( ). Screening was found to be cost-effective at that cost if it reduced DKA events at diagnosis by 20% and resulted in a 0.1% improvement in lifetime A1C ( ). Although there are potential benefits to screening and identifying individuals with early-stage disease, type 1 diabetes screening also has been shown to have potential negative outcomes, including increased anxiety for patients and their family members ( ) and misunderstanding about type 1 diabetes risk ( , ). Additionally, monitoring of individuals with stage 1 or stage 2 disease is needed to realize the potential benefits of type 1 diabetes screening; such monitoring can be burdensome, and not all patients will comply with ongoing testing ( ). Furthermore, autoantibody screening may need to be performed at multiple ages to best identify at-risk individuals and those with early-stage diabetes ( , ). Currently, type 1 diabetes screening recommendations and some research efforts primarily focus on screening at-risk family members or those with elevated genetic risk ( , ). Given that nearly 90% of patients with type 1 diabetes do not have a family history of type 1 diabetes ( ), population screening for this disease is actively being performed in research programs, such as Fr1da in Germany ( ) and Autoimmunity Screening for Kids in the United States ( ); has been proposed by law across Italy ( ); and is being discussed as a potential strategy to broaden identification of at-risk individuals clinically ( , , ). Should population screening for type 1 diabetes via autoantibody testing be undertaken, models that engage pediatrics, including screening at well-child visits, will be needed. this disease is actively being performed in research programs, such as Fr1da in Germany ( ) and Autoimmunity Screening for Kids in the United States ( ); has been proposed by law across Italy ( ); and is being discussed as a potential strategy to broaden identification of at-risk individuals clinically ( , , ). Should population screening for type 1 diabetes via autoantibody testing be undertaken, models that engage pediatrics, including screening at well-child visits, will be needed. Primary pediatric care and, in particular, routine well-child visits are integral to existing preventive care and pediatric screening efforts such as those for lead, familial hypercholesterolemia, and anemia ( ). Few type 1 diabetes screening efforts have engaged primary care clinicians or explored integrating screening into existing pediatric workflows ( ). Here, we used qualitative interviews with multiple constituents, including parents, clinicians (endocrinology and pediatrics), and health insurers, and surveys with primary care pediatricians to explore barriers to and facilitators of type 1 diabetes autoantibody screening in pediatric primary care using the Practical, Robust Implementation and Sustainability Model (PRISM) ( ). We also sought to examine the Conceptual Model of Implementation Research (CMIR) implementation outcomes of acceptability (the perception that screening is agreeable, pleasing, or satisfactory), appropriateness (the perceived fit, relevance, or compatibility of screening), and feasibility (the extent to which screening could be successfully implemented) ( ) of population-based type 1 diabetes screening in pediatrics. Multiple constituents who may be affected by or responsible for implementation of type 1 diabetes screening in pediatrics, including parents, clinicians, and insurers, were engaged to better understand barriers, facilitators, and perspectives ( ). Although prior research has characterized general barriers to type 1 diabetes screening from endocrinology clinicians’ perspectives ( ), understanding implementation outcomes and barriers to and facilitators of type 1 diabetes screening during well-child visits in primary care provides key insights to the potential pitfalls and strategies to ensure the successful, sustainable, and efficient implementation in this setting. Research Design and Methods Study Setting Geisinger, an integrated health care system in central Pennsylvania, provides care for ∼1 million patients annually via multiple hospitals and outpatient facilities. Annually, >450,000 pediatric visits are completed by pediatric primary care clinicians in 21 clinics. As a learning health system, Geisinger aims to continuously innovate to improve patient care ( ). Geisinger also insures ∼40% of its patients with coverage by the Geisinger Health Plan. As an integrated health system, the health plan and health care network work together to promote quality care ( ) and make coverage decisions. Study Design This study was guided by the implementation science models PRISM and CMIR and, using mixed methods, aimed to solicit multilevel perspectives from patients, clinicians, and health insurers on barriers to and facilitators of population-based type 1 diabetes autoantibody screening in pediatric well-child visits, as well as assess the pre-implementation outcomes of acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility ( , , ). This study was reviewed and approved by the Geisinger Institutional Review Board (Danville, PA) (IRB 2022-0853), and all interview and survey participants provided informed consent. Data Collection Semi-Structured Qualitative Interviews We conducted semi-structured interviews with parents of pediatric patients, Geisinger clinicians (endocrinologists and general pediatricians), and health insurers between June 2023 and January 2024. We developed similar but separate semi-structured interview guides for parents, clinicians, and health insurers to assess barriers to and facilitators of screening for type 1 diabetes at well-child visits in pediatrics ( Supplementary Material ). The interview guides included questions about screening in general and screening for type 1 diabetes and several questions comparing screening for type 1 diabetes to screening for familial hypercholesterolemia. Unlike type 1 diabetes, familial hypercholesterolemia is a condition that currently has guidelines for population screening (in patients 9–11 years of age) ( ). The interview guides were developed by reviewing the current literature, including adapting questions pertinent to PRISM domains ( ) and in collaboration with the qualitative team. To recruit interview participants, contact information for parents (≥18 years of age) of all children (<18 years of age) seen at a Geisinger pediatric practice site within the past 2 years was identified via an electronic data pull of patients’ emergency contact information. A random list of 200 families with equal distribution across child age-groups (<5, 5–11, and 12–17 years) was generated and used to recruit parents. All currently practicing Geisinger clinicians (i.e., physicians, physician associates, and nurse practitioners) in general pediatrics and pediatric endocrinology were recruited via e-mail. Clinician learners, including residents and fellows, were not included in recruitment. Individuals working in leadership roles at Geisinger Health Plan who were recommended to the study team were recruited via e-mail. Interviews were conducted until thematic saturation occurred for parents and clinicians or until recruitment attempts were exhausted for insurers ( ). Interviews were conducted until thematic saturation occurred for parents and clinicians or until recruitment attempts were exhausted for insurers ( ). The interviews were conducted virtually via phone or the Microsoft Teams video conferencing platform by three faculty researchers (K.M.R., E.A.V., and J.M.S.), a genetic counselor (J.G.), two medical students (A.E.B. and L.I.), and a project coordinator (N.W.) trained in qualitative data collection. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and de-identified. Parents were provided with an overview of type 1 diabetes and familial hypercholesterolemia at the beginning of the interview, and clinicians and insurers were provided a summary, if requested; details regarding type 1 diabetes screening were not reviewed ( Supplementary Material ). Demographic information was obtained from participants. All individuals were offered a $25 gift card for their participation. Primary Care Pediatrician Survey Because clinician interviews were conducted with both endocrinologists and primary care pediatricians, a clinician survey was conducted to further assess the acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility of type 1 diabetes screening among pediatric primary care clinicians at Geisinger. These clinicians are key to implementation of any primary care screening strategies in pediatrics and, as such, their perspectives on these leading indicators of implementation success ( , ) are vital to understanding the potential of type 1 diabetes screening at well-child visits. The survey leveraged several validated scales, including the Acceptability of Implementation Measure (AIM), Intervention Appropriateness Measure (IAM), and Feasibility of Intervention Measure (FIM) ( ) ( Supplementary Material ). These measures were used to capture acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility of screening for two conditions: type 1 diabetes and familial hypercholesterolemia, a condition currently recommended for screening at well-child visits for patients aged 9–11 years ( ) ( Supplementary Material ). Respondents were able to expand on their responses using free text. An electronic REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture) survey ( , ) was sent to 76 Geisinger general pediatric clinicians practicing at the time of survey distribution (63 physicians, 8 nurse practitioners, and 5 physician associates) via e-mail and was deployed for 30 days in September and October 2023. Clinicians were not selected based on prior performance of type 1 diabetes screening, and data on prior experience performing screening were not collected. Survey participants were offered a $10 gift card for their participation. Data Analysis Semi-Structured Qualitative Interviews The interview facilitator documented a summary immediately after each semi-structured interview. The summaries provided a mechanism for high-level analysis during data collection, allowed for iterative improvement of the semi-structured interview guides, facilitated initial codebook development, and minimized the number of de novo codes that required re-review and re-coding of transcripts during data analysis ( , ). Transcripts were initially coded in Microsoft Word software using an a priori codebook developed from the interview summaries, expected themes, and implementation outcomes ( ). The codebook and code definitions were iteratively updated as deductive qualitative analysis progressed. A multidisciplinary coding team with members trained in qualitative analysis was formed, consisting of four initial coders from research, clinical service delivery, and academia (C.G.K., J.G., E.A.V., and J.M.S.). Coding occurred using a primary/secondary coding scheme, through which one member of the team coded a transcript and then electronically sent it to a secondary coder, who either agreed or disagreed with assigned codes and/or added additional codes ( ). Discrepancies were resolved during research meetings by the broader qualitative study team (C.G.K., G.C.-S., J.G., K.M.R., E.A.V., J.M.S., and L.K.J.) until consensus was reached. Finalized consensus-coded transcripts were then put into NVivo software for data management and for ease of refining data analysis. Data for each code were exported from NVivo and summarized, categorizing data into themes and subthemes for each constituent group (parents, clinicians, and health insurers), as appropriate. Themes were further described and mapped to PRISM domains ( ), and exemplar quotes were selected by the coding team. Primary Care Pediatrician Surveys Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographics and survey measures. An average score across the different measures within each validated scale was calculated (e.g., the average of the four AIM items). Partial responses with at least one completed measure (AIM, IAM, or FIM) were included in the analysis. Cronbach’s α was calculated to assess agreement between the sub-measures. Wilcoxon signed rank tests were computed for the AIM, IAM, and FIM scales between type 1 diabetes and familial hypercholesterolemia. Analyses were conducted in R, v. 4.4.1, statistical software ( ). Results Participant Characteristics Semi-Structured Interview Participant Demographics One-hundred and seventy-four parents were contacted and invited to participate in an interview. Thirty-four agreed to participate, and 26 completed an interview. Eighty-one general pediatric physicians and advanced practice providers were invited to participate in an interview. Seven completed an interview, one agreed to participate but failed to schedule an interview, nine declined participation, and 64 did not respond to the study invitation. In addition to general pediatrics clinicians, five pediatric endocrinology physicians and advanced practice providers were invited to participate. Three completed an interview, and two did not respond to the study invitation. Seven insurance leaders were identified via recommendation to the study team and invited to participate. Two completed an interview, one declined participation, and four did not respond to the study invitation. Interviews ranged in length from 17.5 to 90.8 minutes, with an average length of 37.9 minutes. Demographic characteristics of parent and clinician/insurer interview participants are summarized in Supplementary Table S1 . Demographic characteristics of those declining participation and nonresponders are unknown. Four parents knew someone with type 1 diabetes and thus had some experience with the condition. Primary Care Pediatrician Survey Participant Demographics Fifteen general pediatrics clinicians participated in the survey (response rate 19.7%), two of whom only partially completed the survey. Both partial responses were included in the analysis. One partial responder completed all three standard measures, and the other completed only the AIM and IAM scales. Demographic characteristics of the survey participants are summarized in Supplementary Table S1 . The majority of participants (10 of 13 [77%]) were women, and the average age was 49.1 years (range 36–69 years). Ten of the respondents were physicians, three were nurse practitioners, and two did not specify their discipline. There was a wide distribution in experience among the respondents, with six having ≤10 years of experience, seven with >10 years of experience, and two who did not specify their years of experience. Parent Views on Acceptability and Appropriateness Most parents interviewed indicated that they viewed type 1 diabetes screening as acceptable and appropriate. Parents described positive views toward screening because of its potential to improve their child’s health or ability to seek treatment, the opportunity it presented to delay disease onset or prevent complications, and, in the setting of negative results, its potential to afford peace of mind. Barriers and Facilitators Barriers to and facilitators of screening are summarized in with more detailed subthemes and illustrative quotes in and for parents and and for clinicians. Barriers and facilitators are mapped to PRISM domains ( ) and organized based on the five domains described below. Program (Intervention) From the Parent Perspective Type 1 diabetes autoantibody screening requires a blood sample. Although about one-third of parents expressed no concerns regarding testing via a blood draw, several parents did express unease regarding the pain, invasiveness, and repetition of blood work for type 1 diabetes screening. The age of the child affected this concern, with more significant apprehension about blood draws for younger children. Clinicians also mentioned the challenges involved in conducting blood draws on children, noting that parental discomfort with the difficulty of blood draws or the distress of the test for the child was a barrier. Clinicians mentioned several variables that could influence a child’s tolerance of a blood draw, including time of day, understanding of the test, and temperament of the child. Parents and clinicians mentioned that conducting the blood draw for screening coupled with other blood draws would make screening easier to adopt. Parental perspectives on the burden of screening costs were an important factor for parents when considering screening. Importantly, parents reflected that parental characteristics could further exacerbate cost as a barrier because cost not only includes the cost of the test, but also the cost of missing work to attend a scheduled visit. Many parents also described the potential for false-positive or false-negative screening test results to prompt fear and anxiety, thus decreasing interest in completing the screening. Many parents also described the potential for false-positive or false-negative screening test results to prompt fear and anxiety, thus decreasing interest in completing the screening. Characteristics of Organizational Recipients of the Intervention (Type 1 Diabetes Screening) Parents identified scheduling within the health care system as a major barrier to completing type 1 diabetes screening. Parents noted that limited staffing availability and health care resources and complexity of family work and school schedules could further increase scheduling barriers. Similarly, clinicians mentioned the limitation of health care staffing and how it could hinder implementation of type 1 diabetes screening. Clinicians mentioned that their time is a limited resource, especially when patients have other health concerns of higher priority. In addition, appropriate staff members, including phlebotomists with pediatric experience, may not be available to accommodate blood draws onsite. Clinicians also noted that electronic health record (EHR) systems, although intended to facilitate care, can be a barrier to screening because of inefficiencies that further limit clinician time or introduce logistical hurdles to screening. Characteristics of Parent Recipients of the Intervention (Type 1 Diabetes Screening) Parents mentioned a lack of education and understanding related to screening for type 1 diabetes as a barrier to screening. Parents’ views on type 1 diabetes, its associated disease burden, and its management (e.g., insulin pump technology) were described as a potential barrier to screening. Parents reflected a fear of a positive result given their views on a type 1 diabetes diagnosis. Personal beliefs are an important aspect to decision-making in health care. Here, parents mentioned cultural, political, and religious beliefs acting as a barrier to adopting type 1 diabetes screening, drawing on experience of or knowledge around current preventive health behaviors, including vaccinations. In addition, historical family health behaviors were mentioned to have a strong influence on the level of understanding of the importance of type 1 diabetes screening specifically or health screenings in general. External Environment As noted above, parental perspectives on cost were seen as a barrier to screening. Related to cost, both parents and insurers noted health insurance coverage as an important factor when considering screening for type 1 diabetes. Insurers saw lack of Medicaid approval and insurers’ potential limited willingness to pay for screenings as key barriers. Parents suggested that free screenings or screenings covered by insurance would be more feasible. External guidelines recommending autoantibody screening were also viewed as a facilitator to adoption of screening and would factor into insurance coverage decisions. In addition to health insurance coverage policies, misinformation, spread by word of mouth or through social media, was a common aspect of the external environment mentioned by parents that could negatively affect implementation of screening. A lack of community resources to support education about screenings was also described as a barrier. Implementation and Sustainability Infrastructure Parents, clinicians, and insurers had several suggestions for successful implementation of type 1 diabetes autoantibody screening. Parents felt that appropriate education on the benefits of screening for type 1 diabetes would increase adoption and penetration of screening. An example mentioned as a method of providing education was to send written or electronic educational materials ahead of a scheduled visit, allowing parents to be prepared, know what to expect, and have the necessary time to think of any questions related to screening. Furthermore, parents felt that education coming from their child’s pediatrician would increase adoption of type 1 diabetes screening because a trusting relationship was already established. Clinicians felt that education for parents coming from the child’s pediatrician or clinic nursing staff could also facilitate screening. Clinicians also noted that additional educational materials and resources were needed to provide adequate training for clinicians related to type 1 diabetes screening. Finally, insurers felt that education of both parents and clinicians would be necessary to achieve high adoption of type 1 diabetes screening. Clinicians indicated that resources such as EHR tools and clear protocols for screenings could also improve feasibility of screening by streamlining the process. Identification of a leader championing screening within the system was also described as a facilitator. Incentives were described as a potential facilitator by both parents and insurers. Parents indicated that parental incentives (e.g., a gift card) would increase parental completion of screening, and insurers suggested that clinician-facing incentive strategies (e.g., monetary incentives) could increase adoption. Finally, to increase the reach to parents who may not have access to health care for their child or otherwise cannot get to the doctor’s office, door-to-door screening, school-based screenings, and screening drives were mentioned. Parents indicated that parental incentives (e.g., a gift card) would increase parental completion of screening, and insurers suggested that clinician-facing incentive strategies (e.g., monetary incentives) could increase adoption. Finally, to increase the reach to parents who may not have access to health care for their child or otherwise cannot get to the doctor’s office, door-to-door screening, school-based screenings, and screening drives were mentioned. Comparing Type 1 Diabetes Screening to Screening for Familial Hypercholesterolemia When asked to compare screening for type 1 diabetes with screening for familial hypercholesterolemia, clinicians noted that population screening for familial hypercholesterolemia has support in published guidelines and strong supporting evidence and is already more widely performed. Clinicians reflected that a family history of type 1 diabetes currently should prompt screening, but guidelines supporting broad screening and data regarding the utility and cost-effectiveness of such screening are needed. Finally, several clinicians shared the perspective that screening for familial hypercholesterolemia may be more useful given their perception that the condition can be occurring silently for longer (e.g., until adulthood with cardiovascular disease) compared with type 1 diabetes (e.g., with presentation of symptoms in childhood). Many parents reflected that family history would affect parents’ interest in screening for both conditions; several shared that family history may affect parents’ interest in familial hypercholesterolemia given the monogenic nature of the condition. Several parents reflected more concerns and fear about the consequences of identifying a positive result via type 1 diabetes screening, including the nature of type 1 diabetes and the complexity of its management. Primary Care Pediatrician Survey Surveys using the AIM, IAM, and FIM scales were conducted to assess the acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility of type 1 diabetes and familial hypercholesterolemia screening in pediatrics, respectively, among a broader pediatric primary care clinician population. Participants completed the survey based on their experience, which may have included actual experience with type 1 diabetes and familial hypercholesterolemia screening or extrapolation from other screening experience and perspectives on screening. The AIM, IAM, and FIM items all showed adequate agreement. Cronbach’s α by measure (values range from 0 to 1, with higher values suggesting higher agreement between items) were as follows: AIM familial hypercholesterolemia 0.955, type 1 diabetes 0.985, IAM familial hypercholesterolemia 0.980, type 1 diabetes 0.980, FIM familial hypercholesterolemia 0.980, and type 1 diabetes 0.980). The AIM items revealed that, most primary care pediatric clinicians (66.7%) approved of screening for type 1 diabetes at well-child visits and found the prospect appealing (73.3%). Respondents said they enjoyed performing screening for type 1 diabetes (53.3%) and they welcomed the idea of screening for type 1 diabetes at well-child visits (53.3%). Concerns related to the acceptability of screening that were noted in free-text responses included lack of time, limited preparedness for interpretation of results, and unawareness of type 1 diabetes screening. Reasons for supporting the acceptability of type 1 diabetes screening included its importance and the long-term benefits it would provide for pediatric patients. Overall, on the IAM items, the majority of providers found that screening for type 1 diabetes at well-child visits at their clinic was fitting (73.3%), suitable (73.3%), applicable (66.7%), and a good match (66.7%). Concerns about the appropriateness of type 1 diabetes screening included staffing issues and a lack of time. Several providers noted that screenings are important and therefore found them to be appropriate for their well-child clinic. The FIM items revealed that many providers found that screening for type 1 diabetes at well-child visits at their clinic was implementable (78.6%), possible (78.6%), doable (78.6%), and easy to use (64.3%). Concerns related to the feasibility of the screenings included lack of staffing, parental acceptance (specifically related to blood draws), and time concerns. When comparing familial hypercholesterolemia to type 1 diabetes screening, for the AIM, the mean response for type 1 diabetes was significantly lower than for familial hypercholesterolemia (3.83 ± 1.24 vs. 4.30 ± 0.96, P = 0.042). No differences were found between mean IAM (4.05 ± 1.15 vs. 4.35 ± 0.99, P = 0.1975) and mean FIM (3.91 ± 1.38 vs. 4.14 ± 1.26, P = 1) responses. Discussion Screening for type 1 diabetes offers an opportunity to identify individuals who are at high risk for or in the early stages of the disease, decrease occurrences of DKA through monitoring, provide education and support, and enable access to emerging therapies to delay stage 3 (clinical) type 1 diabetes onset ( ). Currently, type 1 diabetes screening recommendations focus on at-risk family members of people with type 1 diabetes and those with elevated genetic risk ( , ). Given that most patients with type 1 diabetes do not have a family history of the disease ( ), population screening is actively being implemented via research efforts

an opportunity to identify individuals who are at high risk for or in the early stages of the disease, decrease occurrences of DKA through monitoring, provide education and support, and enable access to emerging therapies to delay stage 3 (clinical) type 1 diabetes onset ( ). Currently, type 1 diabetes screening recommendations focus on at-risk family members of people with type 1 diabetes and those with elevated genetic risk ( , ). Given that most patients with type 1 diabetes do not have a family history of the disease ( ), population screening is actively being implemented via research efforts and is being discussed as a potential clinical strategy to broaden identification of individuals who are at risk or in the early stages of the disease ( , , ). Should population screening for type 1 diabetes be pursued, models that integrate screening into primary care will be needed. This study observed barriers to and facilitators of screening for type 1 diabetes in pediatric primary care at the patient, clinician, and health insurer level. Importantly, few studies have characterized such multilevel perspectives regarding integration of screening in pediatrics. Most parents interviewed and primary care pediatrics clinicians surveyed felt that screening for type 1 diabetes at well-child visits would be an acceptable, appropriate, and feasible practice to implement. Prior work among parents and pediatricians leveraging a hypothetical discrete choice experiment demonstrated that both parents and clinicians had a high degree of willingness to participate in screening if conducted via their preferred sample type (e.g., blood, urine, or saliva) and location (e.g., same day as doctor’s visit or at a separate, preferred laboratory) ( ). The data generated in this study further demonstrate parents’ and pediatricians’ positive views of type 1 diabetes screening. However, the quantitative survey of clinicians revealed significantly lower acceptability of type 1 diabetes screening when compared with screening for familial hypercholesterolemia. This finding is likely partly because of the existence of established guidelines for hypercholesterolemia screening ( , ), the more widespread implementation of familial hypercholesterolemia screening at Geisinger, and perspectives shared by interviewed clinicians that additional information on the efficacy of type 1 diabetes screening is needed. There were several key barriers to and facilitators of type 1 diabetes screening in pediatric primary care identified through the qualitative interviews that provide insights that could inform future implementation strategies in this setting. First, although blood draws were acceptable to about one-third of our parent population, the remainder had concerns about this method for screening. Studies examining type 1 diabetes screening ( ) and other pediatric screenings have identified venipuncture as a key barrier ( , ), and other methods to screen for type 1 diabetes, such as via fingerstick, may be more acceptable to parents and clinicians ( ). Opportunistic screening ( ) (i.e., screening that occurs within existing clinic visits and when blood is being drawn for other laboratory tests) offers a potential model for population-wide type 1 diabetes screening within pediatric clinics without the need for an additional blood draw. Such an approach has been suggested for other pediatric screenings ( , ) and could reduce the perceived barrier of a blood draw. As with other screening and preventive health efforts ( ), education was found to be essential to type 1 diabetes screening adoption and acceptability at both the parent and clinician levels, with lack of knowledge about type 1 diabetes seen as a barrier and timely education around the condition and screening seen as a facilitator. Interventions that include patient and provider education have been demonstrated to increase rates of other pediatric screenings ( ). Although additional research will be needed to assess optimal education strategies, these data further highlight that clinician and parent educational resources are needed to enable implementation of type 1 diabetes screening in primary care ( ). Furthermore, other barriers identified by parents through this study and prior work ( ), including concerns about test accuracy, could potentially be mitigated via education. Parental fear of the consequences of a positive result was also described as a barrier to screening. Parent education before screening could provide more information regarding type 1 diabetes and management should results be positive. Ultimately, however, fear of positive results may prevent some parents from pursuing testing. This finding and prior research indicating that positive type 1 diabetes autoantibody screening can increase anxiety for patients and their family members ( ) underscore the need to ensure that supports exist for parents after screening ( ). Accessibility was also an important barrier to screening within pediatric primary care. Consistent with prior work examining patient and endocrinology provider perspectives on autoantibody screening for type 1 diabetes ( , ), insurance coverage and costs were important considerations for parents, clinicians, and insurers. This finding and prior research indicating that positive type 1 diabetes autoantibody screening can increase anxiety for patients and their family members ( ) underscore the need to ensure that supports exist for parents after screening ( ). Accessibility was also an important barrier to screening within pediatric primary care. Consistent with prior work examining patient and endocrinology provider perspectives on autoantibody screening for type 1 diabetes ( , ), insurance coverage and costs were important considerations for parents, clinicians, and insurers. Although screening is recommended in individuals with a family history of type 1 diabetes and in those with elevated genetic risk ( ), screening is not currently recommended across the general population and is not included in the Bright Futures Program/American Academy of Pediatrics recommendations for preventive pediatric health care ( ), which often informs insurance coverage of pediatric preventive care. Continued research and guidance for screening could improve insurance coverage and further increase adoption and penetration of screening by reducing cost barriers and facilitating clinician ordering. Also, affecting accessibility from both parent and clinician perspectives were limitations in available health care staffing, resources, and time. As noted above, screening within existing visits using an opportunistic screening model could increase access to and feasibility of screening by enabling screening at an already-scheduled visit and in conjunction with another blood draw. However, this model relies on using existing visit time ( ) to address another preventive screening. Time is a limited resource and a known barrier to implementing preventive medicine practices in primary care ( ). Implementation strategies that promote screening without increasing clinician time per patient will be needed. For example, clear protocols and efficient EHR tools that decrease the amount of time it takes clinicians to order the screening and interpret the results could increase feasibility and have been shown to be effective in increasing rates of other pediatric screenings ( , ). Limitations and Future Directions Our study was limited to one health care system in Pennsylvania. Because of challenges in recruitment, the insurer sample size of this study was small; therefore, the data presented are exploratory, and future work is needed to characterize perspectives of insurers. The clinician response to the survey was limited (19.7%). For both interviews and surveys, we do not know the demographics of responders versus nonresponders; therefore, we were unable to characterize differences between those who did and did not participate in data collection. Additional studies of broader populations and constituents in other settings will be needed. Such studies will enable additional exploration of perspectives on type 1 diabetes screening in pediatrics. Conclusion With the emergence of therapies to delay clinical type 1 diabetes and evidence suggesting that screening can reduce DKA rates, population-wide screening for type 1 diabetes is being considered. If such screening is to be undertaken, models that integrate primary care will be needed. Tailoring implementation strategies to adequately address the current barriers to and promote facilitators of screening will also be important.
